summary: Fresh sweat is nearly odorless. Body odor comes from three gland types: eccrine glands (nearly whole-body, mostly water/salts, thermoregulation), apocrine glands (armpit, groin, ear canal, areola only; larger, protein/lipid-rich secretion, active from puberty), and sebaceous glands (oil, antimicrobial/inflammatory roles). Skin bacteria -- chiefly Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus hominis, with Propionibacterium/Cutibacterium and Micrococcus also implicated -- enzymatically cleave odorless apocrine precursor molecules into the actual smelly compounds: thioalcohols (3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol, the most pungent), short branched-chain fatty acids (3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid, HMHA, isovaleric acid), and steroid-derived odorants (androstenone/androstenol-family compounds). A 2020 Unilever/University of York study identified the specific bacterial enzyme (a C-T lyase) in odor-causing Staphylococcus hominis that is necessary and sufficient to produce thioalcohol odor, while related S. epidermidis lacks it. Hair increases surface area for bacteria and sweat to collect, amplifying rather than causing odor. Apocrine glands are driven by the sympathetic/adrenergic nervous system (catecholamines/norepinephrine), distinct from the largely cholinergic thermal-sweating eccrine system -- explaining why emotional/stress sweat and heat sweat differ physiologically, since apocrine output rises with stress, fear, and pain, feeding more precursor material to bacteria.
gaps: Did not find a peer-reviewed quantitative comparison of odor intensity between thermal vs. emotional sweat -- only mechanistic/neural-control differences were sourced.

Did not find primary literature specifically on scalp odor mechanisms (sebum oxidation vs. bacterial action) -- scalp is named only as an apocrine-gland-bearing site in the hyperhidrosis review.

summary: A single SNP in the ABCC11 gene (rs17822931, 538G>A) is the master switch for underarm body odor and earwax texture: the AA genotype yields dry earwax and little/no axillary odor, while GG/GA yields wet earwax and normal odor-producing apocrine secretions. This variant shows one of the largest allele-frequency gradients in the human genome — the low-odor 'A' allele sits near ~88% in East Asian population samples versus roughly 12% in Europeans and 3% in Africans (dbSNP/ALFA data) — and clinical studies confirm it as a valid diagnostic marker for osmidrosis. Genotype measurably shapes behavior too: a large UK cohort study found genetically non-odorous individuals used deodorant significantly less, though the effect was partial (most still used it out of habit/social norm). Separately, MHC/HLA immune genes shape odor preference between people (Wedekind's sweaty T-shirt study), skin lipid chemistry changes with age to produce the specific 'old-person smell' compound 2-nonenal (detectable mainly after age 40), and a distinct, serious genetic condition — trimethylaminuria (FMO3 gene mutation) — causes a fish-like odor and needs medical, not cosmetic, attention. No claims here are made about ethnic groups as such; all figures describe population allele frequencies and enzyme/receptor mechanisms.

summary: Body odour is produced when normally near-odourless sweat and skin oils are metabolised by resident skin bacteria into volatile compounds, and diet/lifestyle change what raw material is available for that process. Peer-reviewed trials show meat consumption makes body odour rated less pleasant than a vegetarian diet (Havlicek & Lenochova 2006), and garlic consumption makes body odour rated more pleasant and attractive (Fialová et al. 2016), both judged by independent raters smelling underarm pads. Garlic and onion route sulfur compounds (allyl methyl sulfide) through the blood to skin, lungs and sweat for hours. Fenugreek/curry can impart a maple-syrup/curry smell via sotolon excreted unchanged in sweat and urine. Alcohol is metabolised to acetaldehyde/acetic acid, some of which is excreted through breath and sweat. Ketogenic/low-carb diets raise breath and sweat acetone (a volatile ketone). Synthetic fabrics like polyester harbor different, more odour-producing bacteria (Micrococcus) than cotton, making the same sweat smell worse (Callewaert et al. 2014). Obesity/skin folds trap moisture and heat, favoring bacterial/yeast overgrowth (intertrigo) and foul odour. Stress activates apocrine glands, and the resulting sweat, once bacterially degraded, is detectably different and can carry chemosignal information. Two mechanistic caveats requiring medical evaluation: trimethylaminuria (TMAU, fishy odour) and diabetic ketoacidosis (fruity/acetone breath) are medical conditions, not lifestyle quirks, and should be flagged to a doctor.
gaps: Did not find a peer-reviewed primary source specifically isolating coffee's effect on body odor (mostly breath-odor consumer sources found, not mechanistic studies) — recommend a follow-up search on coffee metabolites in sweat if the article needs this specific claim.

Dehydration's direct effect on body-odor concentration (more concentrated apocrine secretions) was not confirmed with a primary peer-reviewed source in this pass — current claims rest on general sweat-composition physiology rather than a dehydration-specific study.

summary: Food-and-wine pairing science supplies a citable vocabulary for fragrance-note balancing. Tannins bind salivary proline-rich proteins and precipitate them, which is the physiological cause of astringency; industry sources describe dietary fat/protein competing for that same tannin binding as the reason fatty steak softens a tannic red, though the peer-reviewed review fetched here confirms only the saliva-binding half of that mechanism. On taste, peer-reviewed dose-response data show sucrose measurably suppresses bitterness (caffeine, quinine, urea, PROP, denatonium benzoate all drop from "moderate" to "weak" ratings when mixed with sucrose), and industry sources describe the same sweetness-calms-sharp-edges logic explaining why sweet, high-acid dessert wines (Sauternes, Port) classically pair with pungent, salty blue cheese. Ahn et al.'s 2011 Scientific Reports flavor-network paper is the quantitative backbone of the "shared-compound" food-pairing hypothesis, but the same paper shows this pattern is Western-cuisine-specific — East Asian cuisines trend the opposite way — which is a built-in limitation worth flagging rather than presenting as universal law. Flavor experienced while eating is mostly retronasal smell, not taste, which is the direct mechanistic bridge into fragrance and body-odor perception. Perfumery's own accord vocabulary (the chypre accord's fresh-citrus-top vs. mossy-dark-base structure) is documented as a real professional example of deliberately built contrast, mapping cleanly onto a "fresh citrus over sweet amber" contrast pairing versus a skin-congruent musk pairing.
gaps: No peer-reviewed source was fetched that directly states dietary fat/muscle protein competes with saliva for tannin binding — that specific fat-competition mechanism currently rests on non-peer-reviewed food/wine industry sites (eddiemerlots.com, tradinggrapes.com), not a fetched primary study; the PMC review (PMC6259628) confirms only the tannin-saliva binding side and explicitly did not discuss fat/food competition when fetched.

Could not find or fetch a peer-reviewed source stating sweetness suppresses saltiness specifically — the one peer-reviewed source fetched on salt/sweet interaction (PMC12231224) found only the reverse effect (sweetness lowers the detection threshold for saltiness, i.e. enhancement), so the 'sweet wine tames salty/pungent cheese' claim is supported here by the well-evidenced bitterness-suppression literature and by industry (non-peer-reviewed) cheese-pairing sources, not by a peer-reviewed saltiness-suppression study.

Harrington's congruent-vs-contrast pairing framework could only be sourced via secondary summaries (Amazon listing, Semantic Scholar abstract page) and a paywalled ScienceDirect article (403 Forbidden) — the primary book/article text itself was not directly quotable.

No peer-reviewed perfumery-science source (e.g. a chemosensory journal) was located discussing accord contrast/congruence theory in formal terms; the chypre-accord quote comes from an industry trade magazine (Moellhausen), which is reasonable for describing professional practice but is not peer-reviewed.

Did not find a direct peer-reviewed statement connecting fragrance/musk 'congruent with skin odor' pairing to a specific olfactory or dermatological mechanism — this is a plausible analogy extension for the article's narrative, not yet a cited scientific claim, and should be written as illustrative framing rather than a hard finding.

summary: Practical guidance from perfumers, fragrance editors, and one peer-reviewed psychology study converges on a few defensible mechanisms: fragrance and body odor mix into one perceived scent (not two separate smells), so notes interact with skin oil, pH, and heat rather than sitting on top of it. Oily/warm/sweaty skin holds fragrance molecules longer and amplifies them, so editors and perfumers steer that profile toward lighter, fresher, greener, citrus/aquatic notes and lower concentrations (EDT over EDP) to avoid an overwhelming or 'sour' result, especially in heat. Dry skin evaporates top notes fast and is steered toward rich, heavy, slow-evaporating base notes (sandalwood, amber, vanilla, oud) plus a moisturizer under the spray. Acidic skin is reported to sharpen and brighten top notes (citrus, bergamot), while less-acidic/alkaline skin softens them and pushes the scent toward its base faster. A real peer-reviewed study shows people's own preferred perfume, blended with their own body odor, is rated more pleasant than the same body odor blended with a randomly assigned perfume of equal quality — supporting the 'find what pairs with you' framing over 'mask what's there.' The 'skin scent' category (Molecule 01, Glossier You) is explicitly built on the enhance-not-mask philosophy, using molecules like Iso E Super that blend with individual chemistry. All of this is editorial/perfumer convention and one specific study, not a large body of controlled dermatological science — flagged clearly. TMAU (fish-odor syndrome) is flagged as a real diagnosable medical condition requiring a doctor, not a fragrance problem.

summary: Personal color analysis in Seoul runs roughly $80-$160 per session (vs. ~$545 for a comparable US session), fueled by COVID-era K-drama exposure, K-pop idol styling curiosity, and a massive TikTok footprint (375M views on the topic). Tourist demand spiked sharply (one Seoul studio nearly doubled monthly bookings in June 2023, slots gone within minutes), and luxury retailers (Valentino, Miu Miu, Dior) now run VIP color workshops. A real certification economy has formed around it -- one structured 5-day program costs roughly $2,550, well above casual estimates. No dedicated market-size figure exists for personal color analysis as its own category, though it sits inside a K-beauty products market valued near $118B (2025). On fragrance culture: Korean/K-beauty perfumery favors subtle 'skin scents' (musk, tea, powder, soft woods) designed for intimacy over projection, explicitly contrasted with Western/statement fragrance philosophy. Middle Eastern (Gulf/Saudi) tradition is the inverse -- layering oud/attar oils directly on skin, topped with perfume, then smoking clothing with bakhoor incense, producing multiple aromatic layers, rooted in cultural identity and hospitality per the source used. Existing personal-scent-consultation services (Jo Malone AI Scent Advisor, Nose Paris olfactory diagnostic, Scentbird quiz) show the fragrance industry already offers profiling akin to color analysis.
gaps: No dedicated market-size estimate (revenue/won or $ figure) specifically for the Korean personal color analysis industry/service category was found -- only the broader K-beauty products market size.

Could not access noseparis.com directly (403 error) or verify the olfactory diagnostic quote against the primary source; relied on a secondary WebSearch summary attributed to that URL, so confidence is downgraded to low.

Did not find explicit climate-based (heat/humidity) scientific rationale for Middle Eastern heavy fragrance/oud use -- the fetched source (anisha.agency) framed it as cultural/heritage rather than climate-driven; a stronger citation would be needed to make a climate-mechanism claim.

Did not verify certification course costs beyond one Creatrip-linked program (Korea Fashion Psychology Institute); other providers (Amoaesthetics, APL Color, Korea Mikwang) were found in search but not individually fetched/quoted.
Japan's 'skin scent' preference (mentioned in the lane brief) was not separately researched; findings cover Korea only.
